passage: "Aditi, before we talk about prestige," said Gargi, the school counsellor, "which tasks make your hours vanish?" Aditi pushed her hair back and thought. "Not the Physics lab. Honestly, the data puzzles in the newspaper, and debate club. Last Thursday I looked up and it was dark." "And which stream do people expect from you?" "Science. Everyone says marks like mine mean Science." "Do you enjoy the marks, or the things the marks are for?" Aditi laughed. "I enjoy arguing with numbers. That sounds like Economics, does it not?" Gargi smiled and slid a course list across the desk. "Then let us look at what that path involves."

qa.q: What did Aditi say made her hours vanish?
qa.a: She said the newspaper data puzzles and debate club made her hours vanish.

qa.q: What did Aditi feel when she realised Economics fitted?
qa.a: Pleased and a little surprised at herself, since she laughed as she said she enjoys arguing with numbers. 🙂

qa.q: What could Aditi do to test the Economics idea?
qa.a: Try an introductory economics resource or talk to someone who studied it, because a small trial gives evidence before the decision.

qa.q: How might the people who expect Science react to Aditi's idea?
qa.a: They may be surprised or concerned at first, since everyone assumes her marks mean Science, so Aditi may need to explain her reasons.

grounding: A student asks which tasks make hours vanish instead of which stream sounds prestigious, and notices a fit with Economics.

subtype: Approach: following friends into the same stream [Pitfall]
passage: In their small town in Maharashtra, all six of Ojas's friends were taking Science, so Ojas ticked the Science box too, without much thought. On the first day Santosh cracked a joke on the back bench, and it felt like the best decision of his life. But by the first term's Physics test the picture looked different. Ojas stared at a page of forces and lenses that the other boys followed easily. His marks came in low. Friends still gathered at the tea stall after school, and being there felt warm, but Santosh was at ease with Physics and Ojas was not. "Do you actually like it?" Santosh asked once. Ojas did not know what to say.

qa.q: Why did Ojas choose Science?
qa.a: Ojas chose Science because all six of his friends were taking it.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when Santosh asked whether he liked Science?
qa.a: Uncertain and uneasy, since he did not know what to say.

qa.q: What could Ojas do now?
qa.a: Talk to a teacher or counsellor about his strengths and get help in Physics, because friendship is a comfort but not evidence of aptitude.

qa.q: How might Santosh see Ojas's struggles?
qa.a: With some concern, since Santosh asked whether Ojas actually liked it, which suggests Santosh noticed.

grounding: A student picks Science only because his friends did, and finds comfort in the group but not aptitude, so Physics becomes a struggle.

subtype: Approach: talking to people who work in the field [Action]
passage: Kabir, you cannot pick between commerce and computers? Let me tell you about Deepika from the next lane. I am Gurpreet, a chartered accountant, and one afternoon a Class 10 girl rang my bell with a notebook. She wanted to know what a normal day is like and which parts are hard. I told her about audit season, long hours, and the small joy of a ledger that balances. She also asked her cousin, an engineer, and the school counsellor the same questions. Then she put the three answers beside what she had assumed. Several assumptions did not survive. She had thought accountants sit in a quiet office all day; I told her about clients phoning at nine at night. She chose more carefully after that.

qa.q: Whom besides Gurpreet did Deepika ask the same questions?
qa.a: She asked her cousin, an engineer, and the school counsellor.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she rang Gurpreet's bell?
qa.a: Curious and probably a little nervous, and eager for real information, since she came with a notebook.

qa.q: What else could Deepika do to check her assumptions?
qa.a: Watch a professional at work for a day, because seeing a real day shows more than hearing it described.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel about being asked?
qa.a: Glad to help and thoughtful, since Gurpreet tells the story to Kabir as an example of asking real people.

grounding: A student asks a cousin engineer, a chartered accountant and a counsellor about a normal day and the hard parts, then compares the answers with her assumptions.

subtype: Approach: working backward from a career goal [Thinking]
passage: Sumit, you want to be a doctor but you are unsure about the stream? Let me tell you what I did at fifteen. I am Minakshi, and my teacher asked me to draw a line and work backwards, then stood behind me while I did. At the right end I wrote Doctor. What comes just before? The entrance exam, NEET. And before that? Class 11 and 12 with Physics, Chemistry and Biology. And before that? Choosing Science after Class 10. I looked at the chain and laughed. I had thought the stream was a matter of taste, but for my goal it was simply the step in the middle. I pinned the paper above my bed and never argued with myself about it again.

qa.q: What did Minakshi write at the right end of the line?
qa.a: Minakshi wrote Doctor at the right end.

qa.q: What did Minakshi feel on seeing the chain?
qa.a: Amused and clear-headed, since Minakshi laughed on realising that the stream was a needed step and not a matter of taste.

qa.q: What could Minakshi do if the goal changed?
qa.a: Redraw the chain from the new goal, because the same method shows a different set of required steps.

qa.q: How might Minakshi's teacher have seen the laugh?
qa.a: As a sign the exercise worked, since the teacher had asked for the backward line and watched Minakshi grasp it.

grounding: Wanting to become a doctor, a student works backwards to the entrance exam and Class 11-12 subjects and sees the stream is a required step.

subtype: Approach: deciding under family pressure without exploring [Pitfall]
passage: At the kitchen table in Toronto, Xin's parents laid it out: Science, because it meant status and a safe job. "It is settled," her father said. Xin looked at her plate and said, "Okay." She did not mention the art electives she had liked, or that Physics made her feel like a stranger. Nobody asked. In the months that followed her notebooks got thinner, her homework came later and her replies got shorter. Yara, her older cousin who lived upstairs, noticed at a Sunday lunch: "You used to talk about your drawings." Xin shrugged. "It is fine." It was not fine, but there was no plan for saying so.

qa.q: What reasons did Xin's parents give for Science?
qa.a: They gave status and a safe job as the reasons.

qa.q: What was Xin feeling when she said "Okay"?
qa.a: Unheard and reluctant, since she kept her real interests to herself.

qa.q: What could Xin do now?
qa.a: Prepare a calm talk with her parents about her interests and fallback options, maybe with a counsellor, because silent agreement leads to resentment.

qa.q: How might Yara see Xin's change?
qa.a: With concern, since Yara noticed that Xin no longer talks about drawings and only says it is fine.

grounding: Parents insist on Science for status and security and the student agrees silently, so resentment builds and effort drops.

passage: Rohan, you cannot decide between commerce and computers? Let me tell you about a student I taught, Deepika. I am Chetan, her computer teacher. In the summer she signed up for a free coding course and a free beginner's accounting course, both online at home. Every week she wrote in a notebook which one she opened without being asked and which one she had to force herself to open. By the end of the holidays she had finished the accounting course, with all its small tests, and dropped coding at the third lesson. She showed me the notebook in July. It said what I could not have told her: she liked the ledgers. Her evidence was better than any advice I could have given.

qa.q: Which course did Deepika finish?
qa.a: Deepika finished the beginner's accounting course.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel about each course, according to her notebook?
qa.a: She opened accounting willingly and had to force herself to open coding, so she enjoyed accounting more.

qa.q: What could Deepika do next with this evidence?
qa.a: Talk to an accountant or try a harder accounting lesson, because a further trial shows whether the interest holds.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel about the notebook?
qa.a: Impressed and a little humbled, since Chetan says the evidence was better than any advice.

grounding: A student takes an online coding course and an accounting course over the summer and uses which one she finished and enjoyed as evidence.

subtype: Approach: negotiating a shared decision with parents [Action]
passage: Ishan, you want to argue with your parents? Let me tell you how your cousin Aditi did it, and I am Ritu, her mother. When she was fifteen she came to us with one page. Three streams, the fees, the careers each one opens, and her own marks beside them. She said, "Can we look at this together?" Her father had already decided, and I had my worries. But nobody was telling anybody what to do; we were pointing at columns. Her father pointed at the fees. I pointed at her marks. By the end we had a compromise: Commerce with Maths, and a review after the first year. I still keep that page in a drawer.

qa.q: What did Aditi's page compare?
qa.a: It compared three streams, their fees, the careers each one opens and her own marks.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she asked "Can we look at this together?"
qa.a: That her parents would weigh evidence with her instead of simply deciding, so she was hopeful and probably a little nervous.

qa.q: What could Aditi do if her parents disagree with one of her numbers?
qa.a: Ask which number they would change and why, and check the source together, because it keeps the talk about evidence.

qa.q: How did the conversation feel to Ritu?
qa.a: Less like a contest and more like solving a problem, since nobody was telling anybody what to do, and Ritu still keeps the page.

grounding: A student prepares a one-page comparison of fees, careers and her marks and asks her parents to review it together, and a compromise emerges.

subtype: Approach: analysis paralysis over an irreversible choice [Pitfall]
passage: My name is Sachin, and I did not choose my stream; the deadline did. For six weeks I read forums at night. Every answer added another option: Commerce with Maths, Humanities with Psychology, Science without Biology, a diploma, an arts college. My list on the phone grew to fourteen lines. Each choice felt like closing ten doors. Amandeep, my uncle, asked kindly, "Have you decided?" and I said, "Almost." On the last day for forms the school office put me in the default section, because a blank form goes to the default. Not what I would have picked. Not what I would have avoided either. That is the strange part: nobody made a bad choice. Nobody made one.

qa.q: How many lines did the list on Sachin's phone reach?
qa.a: The list reached fourteen lines.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling about choosing?
qa.a: Afraid of closing doors, so stuck and anxious.

qa.q: What could Sachin have done to decide before the deadline?
qa.a: Set a decision date, shortlist two options and ask a counsellor, because unlimited options guarantee delay.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt when Sachin said "Almost"?
qa.a: Possibly worried but patient, since Amandeep asked kindly and did not press.

grounding: A student reads forums, keeps adding options and fears closing doors, so the deadline passes and someone else makes the default choice.

passage: Friday night. I have been so stressed about the stream form that I could not eat. Today I finally went to see Shreya Ma'am, the counsellor, and she told me two things I did not know: some schools let you change stream after Class 11, and many careers accept more than one route. My shoulders came down about an inch. So I do not have to get this perfect. I only have to get it good enough, and check. I chose Commerce with Maths because it fits me best right now. In my planner I wrote in red: "Review after first term." If it feels wrong, I will look at the options again with Shreya Ma'am. Nikita

qa.q: What did Nikita write in red in the planner?
qa.a: Nikita wrote "Review after first term."

qa.q: How did Nikita feel after talking to Shreya Ma'am?
qa.a: Relieved, since Nikita's shoulders came down and the pressure eased. 😊

qa.q: What could Nikita do at the review if the stream feels wrong?
qa.a: Look at the options again with the counsellor and check what the school allows, because a change is possible only where a school permits it.

qa.q: How might Shreya Ma'am see Nikita's worry?
qa.a: As a common worry that needs information, since the counsellor gave facts that lowered the pressure.

grounding: Told that a stream change after Class 11 is possible at some schools, Nikita relaxes, chooses the best current fit and sets a review after the first term.

passage: Note, Thursday, by Imran, football coach. Darshan has been missing warm-ups, so I asked her why. She pulled out a folded grid drawn in pencil: study from three to five, football at five, dinner, and half an hour of games, but only after homework is ticked. "It is pasted above my desk," she said. "Mum checked it, but I made it." I asked what she would do if football overran. "Then gaming shrinks, not homework." For two weeks now she has been on time, and her passing in the drills is sharper. I told her the grid is a good start and that I would like to see it again once the match season begins.

qa.q: What time does football start on Darshan's grid?
qa.a: Football starts at five on Darshan's grid.

qa.q: How did Darshan seem to feel about the grid?
qa.a: Proud and organised, since she said Mum checked it but she made it. 👍

qa.q: What could Darshan add for the match season?
qa.a: A flexible slot for matches and a weekly review, because the routine will change.

qa.q: How might Imran see Darshan's plan?
qa.a: As a sensible start, since Imran has noticed her arriving on time and sharper passing in drills.

grounding: A student blocks two hours of study, an hour of football and half an hour of gaming after homework in a grid pasted above her desk.
